exchanges.question: Asked Jamie to comment on the recent management changes elevating Doug and Troy to co-presidents, what it means for leadership development and for his tenure as CEO from the board's perspective. Follow-up to Jeremy: how sustainable is the far-higher-than-expected investment banking and markets activity, and how risk-on are the various businesses?
exchanges.answer: Jamie: Marianne is an exceptional leader; the board decided to appoint two co-presidents to prepare them to do far more at the company, which has not changed the timetable; when Marianne learned of the plans she chose to retire rather than stay, and there is no mystery. Jeremy bifurcated the second question: investment banking fees were fine by historical standards but not at peak, there was clearly some pull-forward and large high-profile IPOs and capital raisings contributed meaningfully, yet the pipeline is quite robust and the high-profile activity seems to be begetting more activity, though he will not guide. In markets, revenues have been elevated for some time alongside much more financial resource deployment for clients; the particular set of things that happened in equities this quarter is hard to imagine being repeated, though the backdrop is supportive. On risk-on, the market is extremely risk-on and JPMorgan is a taker of that, trying to balance supporting clients with being appropriately cautious in an environment with complicated dynamics.

exchanges.question: On the strong CCB deposit growth, how is progress toward the 15% retail deposit market share aspiration, and how might higher-for-longer rates affect the pace of share gains? Follow-up: what returns is JPMorgan getting from the branch build-out, AI investments and banker hiring, where is it in the investment cycle, and what does that mean for medium-term operating leverage?
exchanges.answer: Jeremy: wholesale deposit growth was quite strong this quarter and for the first half, outperforming expectations of a fine but less strong year than last year, helped by franchise share gains and by loans creating deposits in the lending environment (BFI space, data centers). Consumer deposit expectations of low single-digit growth this year are unchanged, balancing very robust net new checking account growth against yield-seeking flows, which remain a factor and a bit of a risk given the more hawkish rate environment. There is no change to the 15% share aspiration, which he views as a natural long-term outcome of executing the strategy (primary bank relationships, branch expansion, deepening the product value proposition). Jamie: expenses are a complete continuation of what the firm has done for years and no change should be expected; Jeremy added the firm will always invest, the returns speak for themselves, and the franchise can invest aggressively for the future while delivering exceptional current returns, which would hold even at 15%, 16% or 17% returns.

exchanges.question: What drove the upward revision to NII ex-Markets, and what is the cadence through the third and fourth quarters and the exit rate into next year? Follow-up: why is markets NII guided higher when the rate outlook is also higher, given it is liability sensitive?
exchanges.answer: NII ex-Markets guidance rises from $95 billion to $96.5 billion for the full year; the implied second half suggests a higher exit run rate in the central case, assuming the yield curve follows the forwards and deposit and other drivers match current expectations. The biggest single driver is deposit balances across wholesale and consumer, both the overall quantum and a mix shift toward slightly higher margin; rates are a little higher at both the short and long end, and actual sensitivity is probably a bit more than the EAR suggests because consumer betas have outperformed the model, disproportionately in the front end, but most of the increase is balances. Markets NII is liability sensitive all else equal and would have been expected to fall on higher rates, but the forecast rose because of balance sheet composition, with lower amounts of financed non-interest-bearing assets expected in the second half, which at these rate levels can overwhelm the rate effect. Separately, the equity allocation to the CIB was increased this quarter, moving roughly $150 million of NII from NII ex-Markets into markets NII, a rare case where a markets NII change is not offset in the bottom line, though it is left pocket, right pocket for the company.

exchanges.question: What characteristics are Jamie and the board looking for in the next CEO, and should investors read Marianne's departure as an extension of Jamie's tenure, with a fixed remaining tenure or a rolling retirement date and longer stay as executive chair? Follow-up: what does no change in timing mean?
exchanges.answer: The timing is essentially the same and entirely up to the board; this is a natural change in how the firm goes about succession. The desired qualities include being good at management and people, analytical, detailed, a culture carrier, curious, with heart, grit, soul and work ethic, able to travel and to walk operating centers as well as meet CEOs and prime ministers; no one has all of them perfectly, and the firm is blessed with many culture carriers including two exceptional co-presidents, Jen Piepszak as Chief Operating Officer and Mary Erdoes continuing to run Asset & Wealth Management, across 300,000 employees, 50,000 in branches and 150,000 in operating and call centers. He is fully confident the firm would be fine if he were hit by a truck. On timing: exactly what was said last time, several years or a few years plus or minus, and totally up to the board, not him.

exchanges.question: Year-to-date adjusted operating leverage has been negative despite a strong revenue environment; with the benefits of AI and technology, is there a point over the next few years when expense growth slows and operating leverage becomes more likely? Follow-up: any update on potential adjustments to regulatory proposals such as the G-SIB surcharge and elements of Basel III?
exchanges.answer: Jamie: with great returns and margins that rose this quarter, the notion of forever increasing operating leverage is a crazy notion and part of why banks failed 20 years ago; AI will have gives and takes and cannot be projected, though there might be a slowdown in expense growth maybe in 2027 or 2028; the firm will spend more on marketing when deposit ROI justifies it, some expenses are really investments with good returns, and the ultimate beneficiary of AI will be customers in a competitive market, otherwise margins would be 80% today from 20 years of computerization. On regulation, four obvious changes: remove the double count in operational risk capital, remove the double count in market risk capital (the firm holds $80 billion or more of market risk capital versus a biggest-ever quarterly loss of $1.4 billion and a CCAR market loss of about $14 billion or $15 billion), adjust the G-SIB as intended going back to 2015, and make short-term wholesale funding treatment fair to everybody; regulators should do the numbers the right way and add conservatism explicitly, and he would happily hold 10% more capital if asked rather than have numbers falsely done. Jeremy: the short-term wholesale funding change, by removing RWA from the denominator of its contribution to the G-SIB score, disproportionately burdens banks like JPMorgan and Bank of America that combine markets, banking and consumer businesses relative to former investment bank competitors, damaging banks' ability to serve Main Street; policymakers should state that outcome if they want it rather than let it happen by accident, as laid out in the firm's comment letter.

exchanges.question: With trading, investment banking, lending and credit all firing, is this as good as it gets, or is there an argument the cycle is earlier given AI, higher global defense spending and supply chain shifts? Follow-up: is there a rate tipping point where deposit behavior changes meaningfully in volumes and betas, which have been better than expected so far?
exchanges.answer: Jamie: it is getting close to as good as it gets and the firm does not know how long it will last. Jeremy: the short answer on deposits is they do not really know; at the start of this rate cycle he would have expected the negative convexity in consumer deposit rate paid to be showing by now and it is not, but common sense says it kicks in at some point. Stress testing considers a true regime change with meaningfully higher inflation and a more aggressive Fed and asks when rate paid accelerates; one should not be naive about higher rates, because taking the current EAR (even though the empirical EAR is probably higher than reported) and ignoring convexity could make a 7% rate environment look great when it would not if the firm had to massively repurchase the deposit franchise. Jamie added the firm does assume some of that; it is in the models and part of the discipline, and the open questions are when it happens and the competitive dynamics of the deposit franchise.

exchanges.question: Challenged the negative operating leverage framing, noting it was positive in dollars with 15% revenue growth and that marginal margins on incremental revenue far exceed the 25% overall margin, and asked why Jamie said this is as good as it gets. Follow-up: with Troy taking over the consumer bank despite no consumer experience (characterised as an FX trader now selling mortgages, cards and deposits), what gives confidence he is the right person?
exchanges.answer: Jamie agreed operating leverage was definitely positive in dollars and that a rapid revenue increase drives a big increase in operating leverage. Jeremy pieced it together: the firm revised this year's expense guidance up by $2.5 billion; consensus built off fourth-quarter guidance implied meaningful negative operating leverage because NII was still working through headwinds while inflation and investment drove expenses; since then the capital markets complex outperformed then-expectations by $6.5 billion in the first half with $1.5 billion of additional associated expense booked, so $1.5 billion of the $2.5 billion increase is already booked and about $1 billion is implicitly added for the second half, from which no strong conclusions about revenue expectations should be drawn; returns, which are exceptional, are what matter. Jamie: similar dynamics exist in Asset & Wealth Management, card spend and elsewhere; on as good as it gets, the market is very healthy, active and exuberant with very high prices and volumes, it could get better but he does not know by how much or for how long. On Troy: people are evaluated on analytics, brainpower, EQ, heart and culture; he has shown that in markets and investment banking, which include extensive operations, back office and technology functions; cross-company experience is important because investment-bank-only leaders can let the rest of the franchise suffer; he is excited and has always visited branches. Jeremy corrected that Troy was an options trader, not an FX trader.

exchanges.question: Is the market vastly underestimating AI's efficiency potential, and could banks, like Block after cutting 40% of its workforce, operate with a much leaner, more agile structure over time? Follow-up: what was most exceptional in equities this quarter by product or geography that may be hard to sustain?
exchanges.answer: Jamie: not a sensitive topic; the firm will use AI to do a better job for clients and fully expects huge efficiency in certain parts of the company; there are almost 1,000 use cases today of which about 50 are really important, across risk, fraud, marketing, hedging, prospecting, note-taking, idea generation and document reading, and it is just starting. The firm is preparing to retrain people, has had discrete areas where it reduced jobs by 30% or 40% with most people offered jobs elsewhere, expects more of that, and notes AI will also reach smaller competitors through Fiserv, FIS and other fintechs; it is a big topic at the July offsite and the firm will report back, but the benefit accrues to customers rather than JPMorgan, and one cannot assume ROE goes to 50% and stays there. Jeremy on equities: nothing beyond the heavily reported obvious drivers, including major IPOs, major index rebalancing, very complicated dynamics in the Korean equity market, a lot of activity in Asia and extremely active clients; it could repeat but statistically that particular combination seems improbable. Jamie added this is visible daily in NYSE and CME volumes, hedge fund volumes and margin loans.

exchanges.question: What is JPMorgan seeing on Main Street given perceived fragility in housing and the risk of higher rates, how resilient is the consumer, and is CapEx and commercial lending broadening beyond AI? Follow-up: why buy back stock at three times tangible book rather than hold more excess capital for a rainy day, and what about potential M&A in asset management or fintech?
exchanges.answer: Jeremy: there is decent CapEx and loan growth across the franchise, some of which does not superficially appear AI-related, but he is reluctant to conclude that because AI demand shows up in non-obvious places such as plumbers and electricians for data centers; CHIPS Act CapEx is rolling off and being replaced by direct AI spend. Jamie: CapEx is about $4 trillion a year, AI went from $400 billion last year to $700 billion this year and is projected at a little over a trillion next year, with maybe a little reduction in non-AI CapEx. On the consumer, spend is fine and robust across income segments with a tax refund tailwind, delinquencies are a little lower than expected across FICO scores, recent Fed heterogeneity data does not support the K-shape narrative, a cohort with negative real wage growth is a watch area, and consumer credit performance comes down to a surprisingly resilient labor market. On capital, Jeremy agreed the firm buys back less as the price rises; excess capital is still approximately $40 billion and the firm now thinks it will deploy over time given a bigger, more complex world (security resiliency, hyperscalers, global infrastructure, remilitarization, trade restructuring, government needs with global deficits of almost 4.5% or 5%), it will not tell the market what it will do, and buying back stock is an investment decision rather than returning money to shareholders. Jamie: he made a mistake last time mentioning $20 billion and could do far more or nothing; the goal is to deploy capital at a 17% return, mainly through hard organic growth in every business (including Europe, where share has doubled in areas with room for more, U.S. branches, cards and the Apple business); inorganic options are always considered but never as a substitute for fixing organic weakness; competition includes Goldman Sachs, Stripe, PayPal, Cash App, Block, Chime, SoFi and Revolut; the firm did a bunch of deals this year, most good and a couple not, remains open-minded on adjacencies and data, has skunk works underway, and hopes Chase UK becomes a great European digital bank over time.

exchanges.question: What is the status of the smart cash tool, when and to whom will it roll out, and what did Jamie mean about having to pay more for money over time? Follow-up: how would Jamie sum up JPMorgan's European consumer banking aspirations across the major markets?
exchanges.answer: The tool relates to how the velocity of money will change in a new world; it is still a test case aimed at a narrow segment of accounts where the firm competes for both investment and deposit business, certain tests will come out and the firm will learn what it can and cannot do, and it could be good for customers and for the firm; something will be seen this year. On Europe, the firm never tried to compete in bricks and mortar against local banks, but digital changed that: Chase UK started about 4 or 5 years ago as a complete startup and now has almost 3 million or 2.5 million UK customers, Berlin has opened and Germany is doing much better than expected though not yet profitable, and the platform cost spreads across more clients and countries toward break-even and profitability. Investment products have been added in the UK and will be added elsewhere, probably with credit card; the dream is a pan-European successful digital bank built off JPMorgan Chase's private bank, cross-border clients, underwriting and research strengths, and he has high hopes while being patient, kind of.

exchanges.question: Having flagged excesses in underwriting late last year and risk-on capital markets, what is JPMorgan seeing in competitors' credit underwriting, is it getting crazier, and what is the outlook? Follow-up: with Basel III endgame possibly codified by year-end and tailoring next year, could the industry enter a period of regulatory stability that enhances bank valuations?
exchanges.answer: Jeremy: crazy is a strong word; data center underwriting is a bellwether, where the key risks are power supply and tenants, the firm has a precise framework and has passed on some deals; it is competitive and eager, with some relationship lending to startup data center builders, but these are normal pressures, and the firm flexes for important clients while holding the line on its own risk appetite with an appropriately skeptical view. Jamie: the firm described a very mild deterioration, not a huge one, across a spectrum including aggressive revenue growth assumptions, expense add-backs, more PIK, weaker covenants and more rollover and interest rate risk, concentrated in some players rather than across the board; when the credit cycle comes, performance will not be a bell curve and there will be outliers as in the financial crisis. On regulation, Jeremy said stability is desirable and nonpartisan, the amplitude of post-crisis oscillations may be decreasing toward getting it about right, banks should be guided by their own standards with regulation as a backstop, and he is not convinced regulation is a major drag on valuations for banks like JPMorgan. Jamie: a Supreme Court decision allowing a president to remove officials more easily makes flip-flopping less likely, legislation should be clearer about intent, he welcomes Mickey Bowman and Kevin Warsh reviewing 20 years of changes, a true safety-and-soundness focus would leave JPMorgan with no MRAs, SVB and First Republic were disclosed interest rate risk failures, resolution and recovery does not work, the discount window should be viewed differently, and the system can be made much safer.

exchanges.question: Beyond the volume and revenue-related line, is JPMorgan also raising other expense buckets such as bankers, tech or marketing, or pulling forward spend given the environment? Follow-up: on the increased CIB capital allocation, how nimble can the firm be, is this peak allocation, are internal limits being approached, and is there room to keep allocating balance sheet?
exchanges.answer: Jeremy: there are some ups and downs in other categories, including marketing strategy he does not want to disclose, but the big driver is volume and revenue-related expense; token expense is a trivial number for the first half and for the full year, though meaningful acceleration is forecast for the second half, it was budgeted and is not a driver of the outlook revision, and it becomes an important question for next year and beyond, where the firm's infrastructure positions it to use the right model for the right purpose (not a cutting-edge expensive model to summarise analyst reports) and open source where appropriate, yielding more capacity, efficiency, better revenue or competitiveness. He will not discuss internal limit management; capital allocation is not like giving a hedge fund a pot of capital but the opposite, responding to client demand, alongside passive effects such as higher volatility raising market risk capital and equity market appreciation raising prime RWA; the firm has a ton of excess capital, its primary goal is to deploy it organically, and it has plenty of capital to serve CIB clients within its risk appetite and return hurdles, subject to other financial resource constraints. The system is flush with capital but at the margin less flush with liquidity, and shrinking the Fed balance sheet requires reducing bank demand for reserves and adjusting liquidity regulation, the next item on the advocacy agenda. Jamie: risk standards have not changed, and if some clients self-select elsewhere that is fine.
